Series::max¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::max() const -> Series
Series::max(std::int64_t dim) const -> Series
Series::max(std::int64_t dim, bool keepdim) const -> Series
Series::max(const Series& other) const -> Series

What It Does¶

max() answers one of two related but importantly different questions:

  • “What is the largest value?”

  • “At each position, which of these two values is larger?”

The reduction overloads answer the first question. The binary overload answers the second.

That split matters because the result shape, axis behavior, and gradient rules change with the overload family:

  • max() reduces everything to one scalar winner

  • max(dim) and max(dim, keepdim) reduce one axis at a time

  • max(other) does not reduce at all; it compares peers element by element

If you carry only one mental model away from this page, let it be this: reduction max(...) summarizes values, while binary max(other) selects winners position by position.

Overload Map¶

max()

Reduces across the entire Series and returns one scalar Series.

max(dim)

Reduces one axis and removes that axis from the result shape.

max(dim, keepdim)

Reduces one axis and optionally keeps that axis as size 1.

max(other)

Returns the elementwise larger value between self and other under broadcasting. Forward values match maximum().

Parameters¶

dim (std::int64_t)

The axis used by the reduction overloads.

  • positive dims count from the front

  • negative dims count from the back

  • the dim must refer to a real axis of the source Series

Changing dim changes which lanes compete with each other. On a rank-2 Series, dim = 0 compares down each column, while dim = 1 compares across each row.

keepdim (bool)

Controls whether the reduced axis survives in the output shape.

  • false: remove the axis entirely

  • true: keep the axis as size 1

This toggle is not just cosmetic. keepdim=true is often the better choice when you plan to broadcast the reduced result back against the original shape.

other (const Series&)

The peer operand for the binary overload.

  • other is broadcast against self

  • nothing is reduced in this overload

  • the result shape is the broadcasted shape

So max(other) should be read as a comparison surface, not as a reduction with an unusual second parameter.

Returns¶

Series The returned Series depends on the overload:

- scalar `Series` for `max()`
- reduced `Series` for `max(dim, ...)`
- broadcasted comparison result for `max(other)`

Gradient¶

max() is one of the clearer places to see that forward similarity does not guarantee identical backward behavior.

Reduction Overloads¶

For max(), max(dim), and max(dim, keepdim):

  • only winning maxima receive sensitivity

  • if multiple equal maxima tie inside one reduced lane, the incoming sensitivity is split evenly across those tied winners

  • for the full reduction overload, that split happens across every global maximum in the whole Series

So reduction max(...) is tie-sharing.

Binary Overload¶

For max(other):

  • backward routing matches maximum()

  • gradient flows to self where self >= other

  • gradient flows to other where self < other

  • at an exact tie, the full gradient stays with self

So binary max(other) is first-operand-wins at the tie boundary, not tie-sharing.

Examples¶

The examples below move from the simplest reduction to shape-sensitive reductions, then to broadcasting behavior, and finally to gradient and failure cases.

Example 1. max() with no arguments reduces the whole Series to one scalar winner.

auto scores = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 7.0, 3.0},
    {4.0, 7.0, 6.0},
});

std::cout << scores.max();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=7

The result has shape [], which means this is a true scalar Series, not a row or column wrapper.

Example 2. max(0) reduces down columns, so each column contributes one winner.

std::cout << scores.max(0);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 7, 6]

This example is worth comparing directly with the next one because changing dim changes which values compete.

Example 3. max(1) reduces across columns inside each row.

std::cout << scores.max(1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[7, 7]

Now each row contributes one winner, so the output shape is [2] instead of [3].

Example 4. keepdim=true preserves the reduced axis as size 1.

std::cout << scores.max(1, true);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,1], strides=[1,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[[7],
  [7]]

The values match Example 3, but the retained axis makes the shape easier to align with the original [2,3] layout in later broadcasting steps.

Example 5. Negative dims count from the back.

std::cout << scores.max(-1);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[7, 7]

For a rank-2 Series, -1 means the last axis, so this matches max(1).

Example 6. max(other) compares element by element under broadcasting instead of reducing anything.

auto floor_by_column = pluss::make_series({2.0, 6.0, 8.0});

std::cout << scores.max(floor_by_column);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[2, 7, 8],
  [4, 7, 8]]

The right-hand Series is broadcast across rows. Every position keeps the larger of the two contenders.

Example 7. max(other) and maximum(other) produce the same forward values.

std::cout << scores.maximum(floor_by_column);

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[2, 7, 8],
  [4, 7, 8]]

That equivalence is useful to know because it makes the overload boundary clearer: max(other) belongs to the elementwise comparison family.

Example 8. On an axis reduction, tied winners split the derivative evenly.

auto reduced_ties = pluss::make_series({
    {1.0, 5.0, 5.0},
    {2.0, -1.0, 2.0},
});
reduced_ties.tracks_slope_(true);

auto reduced_winners = reduced_ties.max(1);
reduced_winners.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << reduced_winners << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << reduced_ties.sensitivity();

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[5, 2]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[0, 0.5, 0.5],
  [0.5, 0, 0.5]]

Each row has two winning maxima, so the upstream unit sensitivity is split 0.5 / 0.5 across those tied locations.

Example 9. Full reduction also splits evenly, but now across every global winner in the entire Series.

auto global_ties = pluss::make_series({
    {7.0, 0.0, 0.0},
    {7.0, 7.0, 1.0},
});
global_ties.tracks_slope_(true);

auto global_winner = global_ties.max();
global_winner.reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << global_winner << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << global_ties.sensitivity();

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=7
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.33333333, 0, 0],
  [0.33333333, 0.33333333, 0]]

There are three global maxima, so each one receives one third of the upstream sensitivity.

Example 10. The binary overload does not split ties. At an equal value, the left operand keeps the gradient.

auto lhs = pluss::make_series({1.0, 5.0, 2.0});
auto rhs = pluss::make_series({4.0, 2.0, 2.0});
lhs.tracks_slope_(true);
rhs.tracks_slope_(true);

auto binary = lhs.max(rhs);
binary.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "y=" << binary << "\n";
std::cout << "dlhs=" << lhs.sensitivity() << "\n";
std::cout << "drhs=" << rhs.sensitivity();

Output¶

y=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[4, 5, 2]
dlhs=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[0, 1, 1]
drhs=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 0, 0]

The last position ties at 2, and the derivative stays entirely with lhs. That is the key backward difference between reduction max(...) and binary max(other).

Example 11. A reduction dim must exist. Out-of-range dims fail immediately.

try {
  std::cout << scores.max(2) << "\n";
} catch (const std::exception& e) {
  std::string msg = e.what();
  std::cout << msg.substr(0, msg.find('\n')) << "\n";
}

Output¶

reduce: dim out of range

This is one of the easiest mistakes to make when working with dynamic ranks, so it is worth treating as part of the normal usage story.

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • max() and max(other) are not the same kind of operation. One reduces, the other compares elementwise.

  • dim = 0 and dim = 1 can produce different shapes and different winners even on the same data.

  • keepdim=true changes shape only, not values.

  • Reduction overloads split ties; binary max(other) does not.

  • The binary overload follows broadcasting rules, so shape mismatches fail at broadcast time rather than reduction time.

  • Out-of-range dims throw instead of being silently clamped.

Summary¶

Use max() when you want the winning value itself.

  • Choose max() for one global winner.

  • Choose max(dim) when each row, column, or axis lane should produce its own winner.

  • Turn on keepdim when that reduced result needs to stay easy to broadcast.

  • Choose max(other) only when you want an elementwise larger-of-two comparison.

That distinction makes the rest of the behavior predictable: reductions change shape and split ties, while elementwise comparisons preserve a broadcasted shape and route tie gradients to the left operand.

See Also¶

  • Series::maximum: explicit elementwise maximum surface.

  • Series::min: lower-bound counterpart with the same overload map.

  • Series::argmax: returns winning indices instead of winning values.
